Angle of attack is the acute angle between the relative wind and the chord of the airfoil. [54] As AOA changes, pressure distribution on the wing changes, with more negative pressure on the upper surface producing a relatively larger force on the wing than the positive pressure on the lower surface. [775] An increase in AOA on a wing increases its lift, while a decrease in AOA reduces lift. [805]

As the angle of attack changes, the pressure distribution over the airfoil changes, producing regions of negative pressure on the upper surface and positive pressure on the lower surface. [775] The negative pressure on the upper surface creates a relatively larger force on the wing than the positive pressure on the lower surface. [775] When a wing’s angle of attack increases, the wing experiences an increase in lift; when the angle of attack decreases, lift decreases. [805]

Increasing AOA changes the pressure distribution on the wing, creating more negative pressure on the upper surface and a relatively larger force on the wing than the positive pressure on the lower surface. [775] When AOA increases on a wing that is slipping into the wind, lift on that wing increases, while a decrease in AOA on the opposite wing reduces its lift. [805]

Sky wave propagation uses frequencies 1 to 30 MHz that are refracted by the ionosphere, sending the signal back to Earth from high in the sky and allowing long‑distance transmission. [270] Sky‑wave frequencies are not used for navigation because the signal path from transmitter to receiver is highly variable. [270] VHF navigation signals, such as those from VOR ground stations (108.0–117.95 MHz), follow a line‑of‑sight path and their range increases with the altitude of the receiving equipment. [1162] At an altitude of about 1,000 ft AGL, VHF line‑of‑sight reception is roughly 40 to 45 miles. [1162]

Sky wave propagation uses frequencies of 1 to 30 MHz that are refracted by the ionosphere, sending the signal back to Earth from high in the sky and allowing long‑distance communication with relatively low power. [270] VHF propagation follows a line‑of‑sight path; VOR stations transmit in the 108.0–117.95 MHz band and reception range depends on the altitude of the receiver, about 40–45 mi at 1,000 ft AGL. [1162]

Mixed ice is a mixture of clear ice and rime ice. It has the bad characteristics of both types and can form rapidly. Ice particles become embedded in clear ice, building a very rough accumulation. The table in Figure 10-15 lists the temperatures at which the various types of ice form. Clear Ice A glossy, transparent ice formed by the relatively slow freezing of super cooled water is referred to as clear ice. [Figure 4-17] The terms “clear” and “glaze” have been used for essentially the same type of ice accretion. This type of ice is denser, harder, and sometimes more transparent than rime ice. With larger accretions, clear ice may form “horns.” [Figure 4-18] Temperatures close to the freezing point, large amounts of liquid water, high aircraft velocities, and large droplets are conducive to the formation of clear ice. deployment of flaps or increasing speed, may increase the negative AOA of the tail. With ice on the tailplane, it may stall after full or partial deployment of flaps. [Figure 4-23] Rime Ice A rough, milky, opaque ice formed by the instantaneous or very rapid freezing of super cooled droplets as they strike the aircraft is known as rime ice. [Figure 4-19] The rapid freezing results in the formation of air pockets in the ice, giving it an opaque appearance and making it porous and brittle. For larger accretions, rime ice may form a streamlined extension of the wing. Low temperatures, lesser amounts of liquid water, low velocities, and small droplets are conducive to the formation of rime ice.
